title: 2026 Ford Mustang RTR tanıtıldı
summary: Ford ve RTR Vehicles iş birliğiyle geliştirilen 2026 Ford Mustang RTR, drift odaklı donanımları ve 43.705 dolarlık başlangıç fiyatıyla tanıtıldı.
body:
Car and Driver ve The Drive'ın aktardığına göre, Ford ve RTR Vehicles ortaklığıyla geliştirilen **2026 Ford Mustang RTR** modeli resmi olarak tanıtıldı. Giriş seviyesindeki Mustang modelini temel alan araç, drift odaklı özel donanımları ve daha erişilebilir fiyat etiketini ön plana çıkarıyor.

## Öne çıkan teknik özellikler ve drift odaklı yenilikler

Araç, kaputunun altında standart EcoBoost 315 beygir güç ve 350 pound-fit tork üreten 2,3 litrelik turbo şarjlı dört silindirli motoru barındırmaya devam ediyor. Motor gücünde bir artış olmasa da, Ford'un GT yarış otomobilinden türetilen bir anti-lag sistemi modele entklere edilmiş durumda. Bu sistem, turbo boşluğunu azaltarak gaz tepkilerini iyileştiriyor. Modelde ayrıca 10 vitesli otomatik şanzıman ve GT versiyonundan alınan yüksek performanslı parçalar yer alıyor.

Sürüş dinamiklerinde ise RTR Vehicles kurucusu Vaughn Gittin Jr. ve ekibinin izleri görülüyor. Paket kapsamında elektronik drift freni, daha fazla direksiyon açısı sağlayan yenilenmiş bir direksiyon kutusu, MagneRide uyarlanabilir süspansiyon kalibrasyonu ve Brembo frenler bulunuyor. Görsel tarafta ise Hyper Lime renk detayları, aydınlatılmış ön burun tasarımı ve özel RTR rozetleri dikkat çekiyor.

## Fiyatlandırma ve pazar konumu

Car and Driver'ın paylaştığı bilgilere göre **Mustang RTR** modelinin başlangıç fiyatı 43.705 dolar olarak belirlendi. Bu fiyat, standart baz model Mustang'e kıyasla 8.715 dolarlık bir artış anlamına gelse de, GT modelinin sunduğu donanımlara daha uygun maliyetle ulaşma imkanı tanıyor. 

**Neden önemli?** Model, sekiz silindirli motorların yüksek maliyetlerinden kaçınarak pist performansını ve eğlenceli sürüş dinamiklerini daha erişilebilir bir fiyat seviyesinde deneyimlemek isteyen sürücülere alternatif bir seçenek sunuyor.

source_texts.title: 2026 Ford Mustang RTR Driven: The Base Stang Kicks Up Its Heels
source_texts.summary: This new Mustang special edition is actually affordable.
source_texts.text:
We recently drove the new Mustang Dark Horse SC, which provides all kinds of motorized excitement—at prices that start in the low six figures and escalate from there. This new Mustang RTR, on the other hand, was conceived to provide fun and performance at a much more attainable price point.
The RTR is based on the entry-level Mustang, which is powered by a turbocharged 2.3-liter four-cylinder engine making 315 horsepower. RTR Vehicles is a drifting and off-road aftermarket company—with RTR an acronym for Ready to Rock—founded by drifter Vaughn Gittin Jr. and specializing in Mustangs and Broncos, which has partnered with Ford to create this model.
There’s nothing off-road about this RTR Mustang, but there is a nod to drifting, a competitive discipline in which RTR has won multiple championships. The package includes Ford’s Electronic Drift Brake (also included in the V-8 Mustang GT’s optional Performance package), a MagneRide adaptive suspension calibrated for easier sideways action, and a steering rack with greater travel, allowing more steering lock.
At the introduction, a few of RTR’s professional drifters were on hand to coach us on how to slide this Mustang around a simple cone course. For an old road racer like me, it went totally against my instincts to drive a car in the obligatory sideways, tire-shredding mode. But after a few minutes of conditioning myself to yank the drift brake to get the car sideways and then simultaneously drop the brake and step hard into the throttle, I started to get the hang of it. I even managed two full sideways circles around a cone and steered out of it—more or less controllably.
It was fun, especially as I wasn’t on the hook for the tire bill, but I was particularly impressed that this drifting calibration did not compromise the RTR’s handling on Thunderhill Raceway Park’s compact West road course. In part, that’s due to the use of several high-performance chassis parts borrowed from the Mustang Dark Horse, such as adjustable strut mounts, stiffer front and rear anti-roll bars, and a rear subframe with stiffer bushings. Other enhancements include the Mustang GT’s more powerful cooling fan and its Performance package’s upgraded Brembo brakes with 15.4-inch front rotors and six-piston calipers.
As a result, the Mustang RTR handles beautifully on a road course, with excellent grip and great stability. And with the light EcoBoost 2.3-liter four-cylinder under the hood, it changed direction eagerly. The suspension calibration promoted this agility on the track, and the multilevel stability control made it easy to slide the car while maintaining an electronic safety net.
The EcoBoost engine doesn’t get any power improvements, retaining the stock 315 ponies at 5500 rpm and 350 pound-feet of torque at 3000 rpm. But it does benefit from an anti-lag system that Ford says was derived from its GT race car.
This system is very simple: When you lift off the accelerator, the engine control computer cuts the fuel to the engine but leaves the electronic throttle open. That allows more airflow through the turbocharger and helps maintain the turbocharger’s rpm. Then when you press into the accelerator, the fuel is turned back on, and the throttle goes to your commanded position. But the turbo develops boost more quickly because it is starting from a higher rpm.
At the rpm we were using on the racetrack, turbo lag was never apparent. Helping achieve this was Ford’s 10-speed automatic, which, in Track mode, does an excellent job of keeping the engine in its powerband and downshifting to lower gears while braking for corners.
As you’d expect, the RTR is also visually enhanced compared to the base Mustang. In front, it gets the Mustang GT fascia, with illuminated nostrils and RTR badges. There are also Tarnished Dark Anodized mirror caps, hood, rocker, and rear quarter graphics, as well as the Mustang GT Performance pack’s rear spoiler, plus 19-inch wheels with a greater offset. Optionally, you can also select Hyper Lime–colored brake calipers and graphics.
Inside, the drift brake lever is trimmed in Hyper Lime, as are the seatbelts and stitching. RTR sill plates and a dash plaque complete the look. If the Hyper Lime theme strikes you as a bit much, you can select black seatbelts and gray stitching instead.
Despite its performance orientation, on the road, the RTR is smooth and comfortable. In Normal mode, the adaptive shocks are well tuned for the Northern California pavement we drove. With the quietest setting for the active exhaust selected, the cockpit is reasonably subdued. However, the 10-speed automatic likes to upshift as early as possible, no doubt to help fuel economy, and that can result in noticeable four-cylinder droning when you accelerate just below the kick-down level.
That raises the question of where the RTR fits into the lineup. At $43,705 to start, it costs $8715 more than a base Mustang. That might seem uncomfortably close to the Mustang GT starting price of $48,795, with that model’s powerful and refined Coyote V-8. However, the RTR’s equipment and chassis are closer to a GT with the High package equipment group, Performance package, and Bronze Appearance package, which tallies closer to 60 grand.
From that perspective, the RTR package slots into the Mustang lineup pretty neatly and delivers an excellent driving experience at a useful discount compared with the GT. Not to mention a 26-mpg combined estimate from the EPA, compared with 19 for the thriftiest V-8. With today’s gas prices, even Mustang owners might take notice. Moreover, it is nice to see an attractive special version of a good car that is priced below the average new car transaction price, rather than two or three times higher.

At $43,705, the RTR represents a $8715 premium over a base Mustang.

source_texts.title: We Drifted the 2026 Ford Mustang RTR. Its Old-School Handbrake Is the Star
source_texts.summary: Don't look down on the Ford Mustang RTR and its 315-hp four-cylinder. It's a lot more fun than you'd imagine. The post We Drifted the 2026 Ford Mustang RTR. Its Old-School Handbrake Is the Star appeared first on The Drive .
source_texts.text:
The 2026 Ford Mustang RTR is a lot of things. It’s turbocharged, loaded with performance-package goodies, and tuned to let you have as much fun as possible before its electronic babysitters kick in. But despite its badge and all that implies, the Mustang RTR is not actually a drift car. But it could be.
First, let’s go over the recipe Ford cooked up. At a brief glance at the spec sheet, you might mistake the RTR for just a visual punch-up package, but don’t let the 315-horsepower output fool you. There’s actually quite a bit going on here. Compared to a stock EcoBoost, the RTR ships with a Torsen limited-slip differential (3.55:1), Brembo brakes, an active exhaust, a unique spoiler, a custom suspension, and wider wheels. It even has a unique calibration for the optional MagneRide suspension and, to top it all off, nearly 20% more maximum steering angle.
This all comes at a price—well, two prices, really. There’s a literal increase of $6,520; there’s also the metaphorical weight penalty of about 200 pounds over a base EcoBoost. Part of that comes from the added mass of the Dark Horse’s rear subframe, which the RTR uses; it also lifts the front and rear sway bars and adjustable strut top mounts from the Dark Horse’s Handling Pack. All in, that makes the RTR nearly as hefty as a zero-option Mustang GT, which comes with the 5.0-liter Coyote V8.
This isn’t the first time we’ve seen a fun Mustang built around something other than a V8. We’ve seen turbocharged SVOs, the V6-powered “Mayhem,” and most recently, the EcoBoost High Performance Package. Each time, the formula has been pretty much the same: Offer the performance advantages of a high-spec GT without having to spring for the eight-cylinder upgrade. Not only do you spend less up front, but if you plan to take it to the track, your consumable prices (fuel, tires, etc.) will be lower too. Win-win.
Gittin It
Vaughn Gittin Jr. and his merry band of miscreants didn’t build “RTR” just to go a little faster around a race track. It doesn’t stand for “Ready to Race,” after all; it stands for “Ready to Rock.” That doesn’t mean you couldn’t build the RTR into a race car; that’s entirely within its brief. But really, the RTR is the latest in an intermittent line of cars built for a singular, but catch-all purpose: hooning.
Remember the Focus RS, with its over-the-top all-wheel-drive system and “drift mode” toggle? This is like that, only it’s a rear-wheel-drive pony car, not a ‘roided-out hot hatchback. The Mustang is longer and far more graceful in rotation than the Focus ever was, making it a more natural platform for something that wants to go sideways.
From the description, the RTR sounds like it might be a bit of a handful, but on the road, that couldn’t be further from the truth. In fact, if you set off in the RTR without activating Sport mode, the only tell you’re driving anything other than a base EcoBoost Mustang is the abundance of “Hyper Lime” accents.
It helps, of course, that all the test vehicles had Ford’s MagneRide adaptive dampers (a $1,750 standalone option), but even with the firmness Sport mode adds, the RTR’s ride isn’t punishing. If anything, that’s the Mustang chassis’s sweet spot. The one thing that does get a bit rougher as you dial up the aggression is the exhaust note. It doesn’t sound bad; it just doesn’t really sound like much of anything.
A Different Approach
The RTR may weigh about as much as a Mustang GT, but it wears its surplus weight more gracefully than its V8-powered sibling. The Coyote’s extra mass sits up front, where you least want it. That big engine wants to lead you around; the smaller EcoBoost isn’t quite so insistent. Combined with the RTR’s bonus steering angle, this little thing really enjoys rotating—which, again, sounds a bit sketchy in a car like this, but that’s where the last unique element comes in: the drive mode calibration.
These days, most even remotely sporty or youthful cars have a drive mode that eases off stability and traction control, letting the driver get closer to the limit of grip when the car starts to rotate. Proper performance cars, like the Mustang, tend to have more than one. Here, for example, you’ve got both Sport and Track modes. Typically, Track mode (or its equivalent) is rather lenient, but the stability control will still attempt to intervene before you can get the car completely crossed up.
And at some point during the RTR’s development, somebody dared to ask the obvious question: “Does it have to intervene?” After all, Track mode gives most drivers enough rope to hang themselves already, so what harm would it do to teach the car’s calibration to allow more rear-end tomfoolery? Apparently, nobody came up with a good enough reason not to, and the RTR’s software advantage was born. Couple that with a physical “drift brake,” and you’ve got the makings of a fun, funky little car.
Like, Sideways
If the RTR is trying to defy the “drift car” label, its hand brake certainly isn’t helping. If you’ve looked around lately, you’ve probably noticed that legit handbrakes have gone extinct. Even in most cars with a six-speed stick, you get an electronically actuated parking brake. This, meanwhile, is a manual handbrake that doesn’t function as a parking brake; its sole job is to temporarily break rear traction.
Stupid, right? It is, in the best possible way.
From a purely enthusiast standpoint, there’s no downside. The RTR steers quicker and harder, rotates more before the computers intervene, and looks pretty good doing it. What’s not to like (ahem, besides the mandatory 10-speed automatic)? To prove the point, RTR set us up with some track time on Thunderhill’s West circuit to see exactly what their playful little pony could do.
I don’t think I’m that old, but I’m old enough to have shopped for brand-new Mustangs back when a 315-horsepower, 4.6-liter V8 was the top dog; this 2.3-liter 4-pot even has more torque, but it also has more work to do. Down on cylinders, though, this little Mustang may weigh nearly 300 pounds more than that old Mod-motor GT.
By modern standards, I would hesitate to call the RTR Mustang “fast,” but it gets out of its own way well enough. Pushing all that tire out to the corners gives the RTR an aggressive look, to be sure, but it also increases the feedback you feel in the front end. On a modern performance car with electric power steering, every bit of communication counts. Fortunately, part of that hefty curb weight comes from the RTR’s big brakes. Six-piston Brembos grab the 15.4-inch front calipers; four-piston fixed calipers clamp down on 14-inch discs out back. They work splendidly.
Nimble and Predictable
The RTR’s tendency to rotate works both for and against it when it comes to fast lap times. Turn-in is crisp and rewarding, but the RTR tends to get squirmy under hard downhill braking, and despite its nimble character, it’s still a lot of car.
